svg.text: NFR Speaking Script with LASCSDIO
60 to 90 seconds · pick the 3 to 5 that drive the design · put a number on each · say what you are relaxing
The script (say the ones that matter, in this order)
OPEN
“Before I design, let me pin down the non-functional requirements. The ones that drive this design are [pick 3 to 5],
so I'll put numbers on those.”
L
Low Latency
For [operation], I'm targeting P99 under [200 ms] and P999 under [500 ms], because [user impact].
Tighter (≈100 ms) for typing, in-path or real-time · relaxed for async / batch: give a completion or freshness time instead.
A
Availability
I'm targeting [99.99%], about 50 minutes of downtime a year: replicas across zones, no single point of failure, automatic failover.
99.9% (≈ 8.8 h a year) is enough for background systems · say which you favor if it conflicts with consistency.
S
Scalability
About [N] users and [X] QPS at peak, [read-heavy / write-heavy], so I'll scale horizontally and cache hot data.
Take the numbers from your capacity estimation section.
C
Consistency
[Operation A] needs strong consistency because [reason]; [operation B] can be eventual, so I'll favor availability there.
Strong: money, bookings, trades · Eventual: feeds, counts, search · Mixed: strong write path, eventual reads.
S
Security
AuthN and AuthZ on every request, encryption in transit and at rest, rate limiting; the main concern here is [one thing].
Name the one that matters: payments, personal data, access control.
D
Durability
We can't lose [data]: it's replicated across zones and backed up, and a write is acknowledged only once it is durable.
Strongest for payments, files and ledgers · lighter for caches and counters.
I
Idempotency
Retries will happen, so [operation] must be safe to repeat: I'll use an idempotency key so a retry never double-applies.
Only when it applies: payments, bookings, schedulers, ad clicks. Skip it for a news feed or URL shortener.
O
Observability
I'll track [latency, error rate, queue depth] and alert on [the failure that matters most], with logs and traces to debug.
Name one specific alert, for example payments stuck unresolved or a growing queue.
Numbers to remember
Latency
Standard
P99 under 200 ms · P999 under 500 ms (most read paths)
Tight
P99 under 100 ms · P999 under 200 ms (typing, cache, redirect)
Relaxed
seconds, or a freshness target (payments, crawler, scheduler)
Payment: accept in under 500 ms (P99), complete asynchronously within seconds.
Availability
about 43 min / month
about 8.8 hours / year
about 4.3 min / month
about 53 min / year
about 26 sec / month
about 5.3 min / year
Default: 99.99% for user-facing core paths · 99.9% for background systems.
Avail-first: serve slightly stale rather than go down (feeds, cache, redirects).
Consist-first: reject or delay rather than be wrong (payments, booking, trading).
Consistency
Strong
money, seats, bids, trades: must never be wrong
Mixed
strong on the critical write path, eventual elsewhere
Eventual
feeds, counts, search, caches: stale is acceptable
Delivery tips
Don't recite all eight: pick 3 to 5 and skip the rest out loud.
Put a number on each one, then say the trade-off:
“I'm relaxing [X] to protect [Y].”
If asked “why 200 ms?”: under about 200 ms feels instant and
leaves budget for network and downstream calls.
If asked how you'd hold the tail: timeouts, caching, load shedding,
hedged requests and fewer calls per request.
Two examples, spoken
Payment System
“The NFRs that drive this design are correctness, consistency, durability and idempotency.
Consistency: payments and the ledger are strongly consistent, because balances must always be right.
Idempotency: networks fail and clients retry, so every payment carries a key and a retry never double-charges.
Durability: the ledger is append-only, replicated and auditable, so we never lose a money movement.
Availability: 99.99%, but if it conflicts with consistency I reject or delay rather than risk a wrong balance.
Latency: relaxed. P99 under 500 ms to accept the request; completion is asynchronous, within seconds.
Observability: alert on payments stuck unresolved and on any ledger vs provider settlement mismatch.”
URL Shortener
“The NFRs that matter are low latency, high availability and scalability.
Latency: the redirect blocks the page load, so P99 under 100 ms and P999 under 200 ms.
Availability: 99.99%, since a dead short link is broken everywhere it was shared.
Scalability: heavily read-heavy, maybe 100 reads per write, so I cache hot links and scale reads out.
Consistency: eventual is fine. A new link appearing a second later is harmless; the key must stay unique.
Durability: mappings must never be lost, so they're replicated and backed up.
Idempotency and heavy security aren't central here, so I won't dwell on them.”
CLOSE
“That covers the NFRs that matter for this system; the others aren't critical here. Next, I'll do a quick capacity estimate to size it.”
